newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-S.Africa economy stalling, c/a to improve.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-S.Africa economy stalling, c/a to improve.

text.p: South African economic growth will slow to just 2.2 percent in 1997 from 3.0 in 1996, but the upside will be a sharp improvement in the current account, according to a survey of 28 economists by Reuters.
Economists, who were polled after last week's one point hike in the key Bank rate to a 4-1/2-year high of 17 percent, said an already weak economy would now slow further.
Forecasts for 1997 growth range from 1.5 to 2.9 percent.
"Domestic demand is already slowing but a particular slowdown in private consumption expenditure will be magnified by the rate hike," said Julia Roy, Treasury economist at Rand Merchant Bank.
Southern Asset Management economist Karen Schoeman said the matching one point hike in prime rate to 20.25 percent would prolong the downturn in the economic cycle.
"Where we saw the economy already slowing and possibly bottoming towards the middle of next year, that is going to be pushed out," she said.
For 1998, economists expect some improvement, as the business cycle turns, but the consensus growth forecast of 3.15 percent remains well below the level hoped for by government.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's macro-economic strategy, unveiled in June, had projected growth of 2.9 percnet in 1997 and 3.8 percent in 1998, en route to 6.1 percent in 2000.

Edey Rogers & Co strategic economist Edward Osborn said manufacturing, accounting for a quarter of GDP, was experiencing "a tremendous consolidation phase" as it coped with both flagging consumer demand and increased global competition.
At the same time the mining industry was facing a tough time with gold output set to fall to the lowest level in 40 years in 1996. But there should be some improvement from 1998.
"I think the big structural changes taking place in the mining industry, in particular gold, could hopefully begin to bear fruit from about 1998," he said.
For investors, already wary of South Africa after the rand's 20 percent slide on a trade-weighted basis this year, the lacklustre growth outlook may be another excuse to stay away.
"Growth is going to slow down even more because of the rate hike. That will deter investors, because investors seek high growth rates," said ING Barings economist Hania Farhan.
The yawning deficit on the current account of the balance of payments, however, should narrow sharply as weak domestic demand limits imports and the fall in the rand gives exports a fillip.
The consensus forecast for the current account gap in 1997 was 4.63 billion rand, less than half the expected 10.13 billion deficit this year and compared to a 12.7 billion defict in 1995.
The majority of analysts still see South Africa in deficit on the current account next year and in 1998, when the gap is put at a consensus 4.14 billion.
But Econometrix economist Tony Twine believes the current account should move into surplus next year.

"We believe the fixed investment drive is going to sag and dwindle, bringing down the requirements which are usually concomittant with it for imports and that the current account will go into strong surplus next year," he said.
